note: Compact application of the common content model. Tasks and criteria are authored additions; source_path identifies the existing textbook unit, not independently verified external evidence. Prerequisites are recommended dependencies. Only Chapter 1 has a complete source-reviewed transformation.

units.title: How Language Models Work
units.outcome: Annotate a pipeline with data, learned parameters, post-training and inference.
units.activity: Draw or write Alder’s pipeline: broad data → pretraining → base checkpoint → optional adaptation → released checkpoint → inference with a retrieved manual → response. Mark which steps change weights. Add a tokenizer, an evaluation step, and two artefacts needed by a researcher that an end user might never download.
units.criteria: Pretraining and adaptation change weights; ordinary inference and retrieval do not. The tokenizer maps text to model inputs. Evaluation measures behaviour rather than necessarily updating weights. Training-data documentation and intermediate checkpoints help investigate development. If you put RL after every post-training stage, revise it to a possible method within adaptation. If your diagram labels the entire assistant “the model,” separate retrieval and permissions.
outcomes: Annotate a pipeline with data, learned parameters, post-training and inference.
Distinguish a training objective from a deployment feature.
Identify which release artefacts support running, adapting or investigating a model.

units.title: What ‘Open’ Means
units.outcome: Assess access, artefacts, permissions, and missing evidence for a specific release.
units.activity: Complete the Rowan release assessment in Chapter 1 before revealing its feedback.
units.criteria: Separate what is downloadable from what is permitted. Distinguish missing materials from uninspected documents; name a concrete next check.
outcomes: Assess access, artefacts, permissions, and missing evidence for a specific release.

units.title: Why Anyone Builds Open Models
units.outcome: Compare explanations for why an organisation releases a model.
units.activity: Choose two arguments in the chapter. For each, name the actor, proposed benefit, supporting evidence, and an alternative explanation.
units.criteria: Attribute an argument to its author. A plausible business motive is not proof of an organisation’s internal intention.

units.title: Risk, Safety and the Data Commons
units.outcome: Frame a release-risk argument against a stated baseline.
units.activity: Choose a hypothetical release. Specify the harmful task, actor, available alternatives, added capability, proposed mitigation, and missing evidence.
units.criteria: Compare like-for-like access and capability. Separate evidence of misuse from evidence of incremental risk and from a policy preference.

units.title: The Lineage of Open Models
units.outcome: Explain a historical change using dated release evidence.
units.activity: Select two releases discussed in the chapter. Inspect their original announcements or papers and compare the artefacts they made available.
units.criteria: Record versions and dates. Identify one documented difference without treating later commentary as a contemporary release record.

units.title: US–China Competition
units.outcome: Evaluate an adoption or geopolitical claim without conflating the measures.
units.activity: Choose one claim from the chapter and identify its measure, sampled population, date, source, and a plausible alternative interpretation.
units.criteria: Distinguish downloads, usage, revenue, capability, and nationality. State when the source cannot establish causation or market-wide coverage.

units.title: Measuring the Gap
units.outcome: Calculate a score and a threshold delay from a small documented example.
units.activity: Recalculate the equal and 80%-manual averages for Alder and Birch. Calculate both threshold delays. Explain why “Birch wins” and “Alder fits our manual-heavy workload better” can both follow from these data. Propose one further evaluation and one limitation that would enter your memo.
units.criteria: Equal means are Alder 60 and Birch 70. Manual-heavy means are 0.8×80+0.2×40=72 and 0.8×60+0.2×80=64. Delays are 4−0=4 and 7−1=6 months. The ranking depends on the task weights; the delays answer another question entirely. Test held-out manuals representative of your organisation, inspect consequential errors and repeat unstable runs. The invented sample cannot justify a claim about real models or market trends.
outcomes: Calculate a score and a threshold delay from a small documented example.
Explain how evaluation and aggregation choices change a comparison.
Specify evidence needed before applying a benchmark result to a decision.

units.title: Distillation and Synthetic Data
units.outcome: Trace teacher–student information flow and locate the training stage.
units.activity: Draw two Willow → Juniper workflows: teacher-written answers and teacher feedback on student-written answers. Label the training stage. Design one controlled test of the benefit of teacher explanations. Then write one sentence accurately attributing the Anthropic report without converting its allegations into a proved effect size.
units.criteria: Your diagrams should identify prompts, generated material or feedback, and the student weight update. For the test, use a shared base, matched training conditions and held-out tasks; compare explanations with an answer-only control, reporting token-budget differences. “Anthropic alleged abusive collection by named labs” is supportable as attribution. “That collection caused their capability gain” requires additional evidence. Reward a clear alternative explanation and an explicit uncertainty, not agreement with either company or commentator.
outcomes: Trace teacher–student information flow and locate the training stage.
Separate a company allegation from demonstrated causal uplift.
Design a controlled comparison of teacher-assisted training.

units.title: Security, Cyber and the Regulatory Fight
units.outcome: Compare policy proposals against the same objective and threat model.
units.activity: Compare a release gate and an observatory: objective, covered actor, mechanism, enforcement, possible displacement, and measurable success.
units.criteria: Distinguish a proposal from an enacted rule. Use the same threat baseline for both approaches and identify a trade-off and an unresolved evidence need.

units.title: Synthesis: Where This Goes
units.outcome: Defend a conditional model-selection recommendation using evidence and counterarguments.
units.activity: Write the decision memo below, then revise the weakest-supported sentence.
units.criteria: A strong response connects the task to release terms, evaluation, costs, risks, alternatives, and a condition that would change the decision. More than one recommendation can be defensible.
